CBP rule FR 2026-22735 · Verified 2026-11-13

A foreign importer of record must use CTPAT validation or a CTPAT-validated licensed customs broker from 2027-01-05

In short

  • 2027-01-05 · Rule effective. From this date the updated CBP Forms 3461 and 7501 must be used for each entry and entry summary
  • U.S. IOR: no CTPAT requirement; declare status on each entry
  • foreign IOR with CTPAT validation: may use any licensed customs broker
  • foreign IOR without CTPAT validation: must use a CTPAT-validated licensed customs broker

Who is affected

U.S. IOR: no CTPAT requirement; declare status on each entry

A U.S. IOR is an individual who is a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident, or an entity organized under U.S. law and located in the United States that meets the ownership or real-property test (19 CFR 110.2(a), p. 70005). It must declare U.S. IOR status on each entry and entry summary (19 CFR 141.22(a)(1), p. 70006).

The U.S. IOR test

The entity must, at all times, either (A) have at least 51% of its beneficial owners being U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents with control of the entity, or (B) directly own a significant amount of unencumbered U.S. real property (19 CFR 110.2(a), p. 70005; explained at p. 69981).

"Beneficial owner" is defined in 19 CFR 110.1 and includes a person who owns or controls not less than 25% of the ownership interests, or who has substantial control (p. 69982; rule text pp. 70004-70005).

CBP may verify U.S. IOR status. Factors it may consider include the principal place of business, substantial business activity in the United States, unencumbered physical domestic assets, unencumbered U.S. real property, whether gross sales generally exceed cost of goods sold, and capitalization (110.2(b), p. 70005).

"Physical domestic assets" means cash in a U.S. bank account, U.S. Treasury bonds, and real property, inventory, machinery and equipment physically located in the United States; accounts receivable are excluded (110.1, p. 70005; explained at p. 69983).

foreign IOR with CTPAT validation: may use any licensed customs broker

Any importer of record that does not meet the U.S. IOR criteria is a foreign IOR (19 CFR 110.3, p. 70005). A foreign IOR that is CTPAT-validated and has the right to make entry may make entry itself or hire any licensed customs broker (19 CFR 141.21(b)(1), p. 70006).

foreign IOR without CTPAT validation: must use a CTPAT-validated licensed customs broker

It must designate a CTPAT-validated licensed customs broker to make entry or to act as the importer of record for the entry (19 CFR 141.21(b)(2), p. 70006).

Which entries the rule covers
  • Entries for consumption, including formal entries and informal entries that must be filed on CBP Form 3461 or 7501 (19 CFR 141.21(a), p. 70006; explained at p. 69983). Operationally, informal entry types 11, 12 and 13 and all formal entry types (footnote 23, p. 69983).
  • The rule also requires a licensed customs broker to verify that a client is a U.S. IOR before making the U.S. IOR declaration for that client (19 CFR 111.29(a)(2), pp. 70005-70006).

What you need to do

Rule text: 19 CFR 141.21(b), p. 70006; explained at p. 69983.

1. You are CTPAT-validated and have the right to make entry

You may make entry yourself or hire any licensed customs broker to do so; the broker need not be CTPAT-validated (141.21(b)(1)).

2. You are not CTPAT-validated

You must designate a CTPAT-validated licensed customs broker to make entry or to act as the importer of record for the entry (141.21(b)(2)).

  • If a broker acts as importer of record for a principal that is not itself an importer of record and would qualify as a foreign IOR, that broker must also be CTPAT-validated (141.21(b)(2)).
  • If the principal on the power of attorney (141.46) is not the owner or purchaser of the goods, the CTPAT-validated broker must act as the importer of record for the entry (141.21(b)(2)).
  • Holding a broker license alone is not sufficient, unless the foreign IOR is itself CTPAT-validated (p. 69983).
  • Using a CTPAT-validated broker does not give you or the principal CTPAT benefits (footnote 24, p. 69983).
3. You meet the U.S. IOR criteria

CTPAT validation is not required; you may make entry yourself or designate a licensed customs broker that is not CTPAT-validated. You must declare U.S. IOR status on each entry and entry summary (141.22(a)(1), p. 70006; p. 69984). The declaration is a checkbox on Forms 3461 and 7501 (a "Yes"/"No" in the electronic versions); a party that does not qualify leaves it blank (p. 69984 and footnote 25).

  • If a licensed customs broker that is not CTPAT-validated acts as importer of record, the broker must identify the principal on the power of attorney and declare that the principal would meet the U.S. IOR criteria, and that principal must have a CBP Form 5106 on file with CBP (141.22(a)(2), p. 70006).
4. Consequences of an inaccurate declaration

If CBP determines that an importer of record inaccurately declared U.S. IOR status, CBP may require live entry (an entry summary with deposit of estimated duties, taxes and fees at the time of entry, so release waits for payment) and may discontinue immediate delivery privileges (19 CFR 142.13(a)(5), 142.25(a)(5), p. 70006; explained at p. 69984).

A licensed customs broker may be subject to a 19 U.S.C. 1592 penalty or other enforcement action (19 CFR part 171, appendix B, paragraph (K), pp. 70006-70007).

What the rule text does not answer
  • Whether the rule reaches goods entered, or in transit, before 2027-01-05, and whether the date is keyed to the entry filing date. The rule text states no transition rule for importers; brokers get 60 days (6 months if delayed compliance is approved) to verify clients (pp. 69996-69997).
  • What ACE filers must change in their systems before 2027-01-05. The rule says the updated Forms 3461 and 7501 and their electronic equivalents apply from that date (p. 69984); it does not describe the filing-system arrangements.
  • Whether a U.S. LLC wholly owned by a foreign parent meets the 51% beneficial-owner and control test in 110.2(a), and how "at all times" is tested.
  • How many CTPAT-validated licensed customs broker firms exist. A foreign IOR without CTPAT validation needs one (141.21(b)(2)).
  • Whether CBP will later bar informal entries by a foreign IOR. CBP did not adopt a ban, but is monitoring such entries and invited comment (pp. 69978, 69985).
  • Whether "foreign IOR" differs from "nonresident importer", the term left in place in part 141, for existing bond and agent rules (p. 69979, footnote 6; p. 69982).
  • Whether entries not for consumption, for example in-bond movements or foreign-trade zones, are affected. The text of 141.21(a) restricts only entries "for consumption".

Trade diagnostic

Trade diagnostic, $495: your entity's U.S. IOR / foreign IOR status under 19 CFR 110.2, and the entry arrangements available under 19 CFR 141.21(b) or, for a U.S. IOR, 19 CFR 141.22(a).

Who does it

Start with a conflict check

IEEPA refunds

Were you the importer of record on entries that paid IEEPA duties? CBP pays an IEEPA refund to the importer of record by default (19 CFR 24.36(b)). See the refund routes.
